hints: Look closely at the shape and staining of the nucleus in each labelled cell compared to the small pale red blood cells around them.
Recall which phagocyte has a multi-lobed nucleus and pale cytoplasm, and which lymphocyte has a single large round dark nucleus with very little cytoplasm.
walkthrough:
Reading Nuclear Shape**
Cell A has pale cytoplasm and a dark nucleus divided into several connected lobes. That lobed appearance is the classic sign of a neutrophil, also called a polymorphonuclear granulocyte. Cell B is smaller with a single, large, round, very darkly stained nucleus that almost fills the cell with only a thin rim of cytoplasm.

Linking Structure to Cell Type**
The small round cell with a dense nucleus and little cytoplasm is a lymphocyte. So A is the lobed phagocyte for non-specific defence and B is the lymphocyte for specific immune responses.
Final answer: A - neutrophil / polymorphonuclear leucocyte / granulocyte; B - lymphocyte.

hints: Start from where lymph comes from - fluid forced out of blood capillaries into tissues, then drained into lymph vessels after cells have exchanged materials with it.
Think about what tissue cells take from that fluid and add to it, and whether large cells like red blood cells can easily leave the capillary.
walkthrough:
Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide**
Blood in the aorta is freshly oxygenated with low carbon dioxide. As blood passes through capillaries, oxygen diffuses out to respiring tissue cells and carbon dioxide diffuses in from the cells. Tissue fluid and therefore lymph formed from it will have less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than aortic blood.

Red Blood Cells**
Red blood cells are large cells that normally stay inside capillaries. Only plasma, dissolved substances and a few white blood cells filter out to form tissue fluid. Lymph therefore contains far fewer red blood cells than blood in the aorta.
Final answer: oxygen - lower; carbon dioxide - higher; red blood cells - lower.

hints: Think about where lymph goes and what cells it meets there when a pathogen is present.
Remember the chemical nature of the defence molecules released by activated lymphocytes - what type of biological molecule are they?
walkthrough:
Activation in the Lymph System**
Pathogens and their antigens are carried in lymph to lymph nodes where they meet lymphocytes. This triggers a specific immune response with clonal selection and activation of B and T lymphocytes.

Protein Release**
Activated plasma cells secrete large quantities of antibodies, and activated cells also release cytokines. Antibodies and cytokines are proteins, so their increased concentration raises the total protein concentration of the lymph.
Final answer: Immune response occurs in lymph nodes; increased production of antibodies / cytokines, which are proteins, increasing protein concentration in lymph.

hints: Think about where the heartbeat normally starts and what the SAN can generate on its own without nerves.
Follow where that electrical signal goes next and which chambers contract first as a result.
walkthrough:
Pacemaker Activity**
The SAN is a patch of specialised muscle in the wall of the right atrium. It spontaneously generates waves of depolarisation or excitation at regular intervals, setting the basic rhythm. That is why it is called the pacemaker.

Atrial Contraction**
The wave spreads rapidly across the muscle of both atria, causing them to contract together in atrial systole. This starts each cardiac cycle and pushes blood into the ventricles.
Final answer: SAN emits waves of excitation / impulses at regular intervals acting as pacemaker; spreads across atria causing atrial contraction / atrial systole, initiating heartbeat.

hints: Recall the normal job of the AVN - to hold up the impulse briefly so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract.
Think about what happens if some impulses can bypass that hold-up and reach the ventricles early by a shortcut.
Consider the effect on timing and filling if ventricles are stimulated too soon or too often.
walkthrough:
Loss of the AVN Delay**
Normally the AVN is the only route from atria to ventricles and it imposes a short delay of about 0.1 s. This lets the atria complete systole and the ventricles fill. Impulses travelling through the bundle of Kent bypass the AVN, so there is no slowing or delay for those impulses.

Faster Ventricular Stimulation**
Because the shortcut conducts quickly, more impulses reach the ventricular muscle per unit time. The ventricles are therefore excited earlier and more frequently, giving a faster heart rate.

Poor Coordination and Filling**
If ventricles contract before they are fully filled with blood, stroke volume falls. The rhythm can also become irregular because some beats come via the normal AVN pathway and some via the Kent pathway.
Final answer: Faster / irregular heart rate; no delay by AVN for impulses via bundle of Kent so more impulses reach ventricles per unit time; ventricles may contract before full, reducing efficiency.
